Hearing Harmony

Chord progressions by ear, in levels from I–V7–I up, along the path that fits the music you know: MLT (Gordon and Mullen), rock and pop, jazz, classical, or your own chords. Bass and piano, no microphone, no notation.

Trainer

Choose a path (the kind of music you know best), a level and a question. Then press Start: you hear the key (a short cadence), then a progression on bass and piano. Answer with the buttons. Space plays it again, Enter checks or goes on. Your settings and your last ten answers at each level stay in this browser.

The paths

Each path puts the same chords in a different order. Start with the one closest to the music you play or listen to.

Path Starts with Comes late
MLT (Gordon / Mullen) I and V7 in major, then minor, then IV; the modes (Dorian IV, Mixolydian ♭VII) vi7, viiø7 and the diminished chords; ii last of all
Rock and pop I–IV, I–V, three chords, ♭VII ii and iii, borrowed chords (iv, ♭VI), the 12-bar blues
Jazz ii7–V7–Imaj7 from the first level turnarounds, secondary dominants, tritone substitutes, backdoor
Classical (Hutchinson) cadences, predominants (ii and IV together), deceptive cadence circle of fifths, secondary dominants, mixture, the Neapolitan
Make your own the tonality and chords you tick

The MLT path follows Gordon: I V7 I first, then I IV I, then the two joined, then the same in harmonic minor before any more major (Learning Sequences in Music, pp. 318–319). The subdominant in Dorian and vi (relative keys) are taught with them. Next come the seventh chords on vi, vii and ♭VII, the diminished chords and the other modes, which he calls moderately difficult. Patterns with the supertonic are held back until after all of these (p. 320). The rock, jazz and classical orders are this site’s own. The classical path follows the chapters of the theory text (see Harmonic Progression).

The questions

They follow Gordon’s four stages of readiness for hearing harmony. At stage 1 you don’t notice that a chord changed. At stage 2 you notice the change but not what kind it is. At stage 3 you know what kind it is. At stage 4 you can also guess what comes next (Learning Sequences in Music, p. 305).

  • Did the chord change? Two chords. Stage 2.

  • Name each function (tonic, dominant, subdominant, subtonic…), each bass note in solfège (or the scale degrees or sargam chosen site-wide), or each chord as a Roman numeral. Stage 3. By default the first chord is given, as a starting point.

  • Same or different? Two progressions, at most one chord apart.

  • What comes next? You hear all but the last chord. Stage 4.

  • Which tonality? On levels that mix major, minor or modes.

  • Inversions: the bass, then root or not. Two steps a chord. First name the lowest note in solfège, then say whether it is the chord’s root. With Inversion step 2 set to Root, 3rd, 5th or 7th, say which chord member it is instead. The answer shows the book’s figures (I6, I64, V65, V43, V42).

  • Follow a voice. Name the note the soprano (or alto, tenor, bass: Voice to follow under Sound and options) sings in each chord, in solfège. Turn on Bring out for the same voice at first.

▶ My answer plays what you have entered so far, at any time, before or after checking. Empty boxes stay silent. Named functions play the level’s chord with that function. In Inversions, “Root” plays the chord with that root and “Not the root” puts your bass under the real chord.

Notation. ♫ Show notation (in the button bar, or Notation under Sound and options: hidden, after answering, always) draws the exercise on a grand staff, exactly as voiced, with the notes lit as they sound. The Roman numerals, with inversion figures, appear under it once you have answered. Each chord is spelled from its numeral (V7 in A minor has G♯), and the key signature is that of DO.

Entering answers. Tap the buttons: each fills the outlined box and moves to the next. Tap a filled box to empty it. On a computer you can also type into the outlined box: numerals as written (V7, ii, bVII, viio for vii°, viih7 for viiø7; capitals matter), syllables (do, so), functions (tonic, dom…), r or n for root or not. An answer fills in as soon as only one button fits. Otherwise press Enter (V waits, because V7 also starts with V). Backspace undoes and Space plays it again. There is no text box, so a phone never opens its keyboard.

Under the answer boxes, ▶ 1, ▶ 2… play one chord at a time. Turn on Bass alone and they play only its bass note, which helps with inversions. Before you answer What comes next?, the last chord has no button.

After each answer you see the progression, its key, its bass line in solfège and each chord’s function. ↻ Again plays it once more. Ten answers with eight right marks a level as done; nothing is locked.

Settings

Under Sound and options:

  • Voices. Three: the bass and two notes above it (3rd and 7th of a seventh chord). Four: the bass and three above, voice-led like a chorale (the site’s satb.js).
  • Key. A random key each time, or one key.
  • Tempo and beats per chord.
  • Silence between chords: from none to 5 seconds after each chord, time to think or sing the bass. The chord’s own length is still beats per chord.
  • Bring out: one voice louder and the rest softer (soprano, alto, tenor or bass; with three voices: top, middle or bass), or a chord member wherever it lies (the root, 3rd, 5th or 7th). The 3rd is good for hearing major against minor.
  • Leave out: drop one voice, to hear what the others do without it.
  • Arpeggiate: play the notes of each chord together, rolled, up from the bass, or down from the top.
  • Pan the voices: four voices S +50, A +20, T −20, B −50 (right is +); three voices top +50, middle 0, bass −50. With headphones, each voice has its own place.
  • Spacing: voice-led (the smoothest motion, the default), close (upper voices within an octave) or open (wider than an octave). The Close, Open and Voice-led buttons under the answer replay the current exercise in that spacing without changing the setting.
  • Drone: the resting tone (or the resting tone and its 5th) held low under the progression, to hear each chord against home.
  • Repeats: with Play each: twice, the second time can be in a new key (with its own cadence first). You track the function, not the pitch.
  • First hearing: at tempo, or the first play of each new question at half speed (replays at tempo).
  • Top voice sound: give the soprano its own sound (the electric pianos or the organs) so its line stands out by colour as well as loudness.
  • Voice to follow: for the Follow a voice question.
  • Notes: held, or short and detached.
  • Chord register: the upper voices an octave lower or higher (the bass stays).
  • Chords: the length of progressions on levels that make their own (Make your own, and levels such as F2).
  • Establish the key: a cadence, the tonic chord, or nothing (harder).
  • Inversions: off (every chord in root position), some, or many. This works with every question: Name each bass note then asks for the real lowest note. The last chord always stays in root position.
  • Inversion step 2: root or not, or which member.
  • First chord: given, or you name it too.
  • Play each: once or twice.
  • After answering: wait, or go on by itself (hands-free on a bus).
  • Chords on and Bass on: the band’s piano sounds and bass sounds, or off. There are no drums.

The sounds load from the internet the first time, so start a session while you still have a signal.

For teachers

  • Bass in the band’s bass, chords on the band’s piano. Chords are in root position unless Inversions is on. Voicing is chosen for the smoothest motion; in four voices it follows satb.js’s rules. In three voices the rules are only nearest motion and the root in the bass, with no check for parallel fifths.
  • Minor is harmonic minor in the MLT and classical paths (V7 has si). Aeolian uses ♭VII instead.
  • Gordon has the class sing I IV V7 I in three parts: top so la so so, middle mi fa fa mi, bottom do do ti do. In minor: mi fa mi mi, do re re do, la la si la (Learning Sequences in Music, pp. 318–319). Three voices here is close to that, with the bass added under it.
  • Saving to a class account (Supabase), singing answers into a microphone and more instruments are planned. The plan is in research_notes/ear-training-plan.md.

Gordon, Edwin E. Learning Sequences in Music: A Contemporary Music Learning Theory. 2012 ed., GIA Publications, 2012. Skill learning sequence: partial synthesis (pp. 111–117), the verbal association warning (p. 108), generalization-aural/oral and -verbal (pp. 131–133); same is easier to hear than different (p. 219); tonal and rhythm patterns kept apart (p. 223); rhythm patterns chanted with vocal inflection like speech (p. 101); macrobeats stressed, not accented, and approached with a decrescendo, expression found between macrobeats, anacruses given special attention, weight and flow, displaced energy in rests and long durations (pp. 187–190).; Theory Concepts pages: Keyality versus key signature (p. xiii); tonality “best refers to what is usually called a mode,” the eight tonalities (p. 149); movable-do with la-based minor and the rhythm syllables du de, du da di (p. 105); resting tone and tonic, a tonality in any keyality (p. 150); unitonal and multitonal music (pp. 152, 157); usual duple, triple and combined meter (pp. 175–176); no direct relation between measure signatures and meter, 6/8 as “duple compound” called inaccurate (p. 176); accents and microbeat divisions do not make meter (pp. 176–177); unusual meter, paired and unpaired, intact, macrobeats versus microbeats establishing meter (pp. 179–180); key signatures as do signatures, one signature for many tonalities (pp. 155–156); rhythm syllables by beat function (p. 86); time-value names lead to counting (p. 38); writing tonal patterns from a familiar do signature (p. 125); letter names and time-value names as the alphabet of music (pp. 36–37); interval names learned in context of tonality and keyality (p. 65); the raised seventh of harmonic minor as si (p. 70); mi si ti re as a harmonic minor dominant pattern (p. 100).; Course pages (glossary, enrichment): audiation defined and compared with imitation (Introduction; pp. 3, 9); notation as a window (p. 8); patterns as units of meaning (pp. 99–100); the aural/oral level and the pause (pp. 101–102); discrimination and inference learning, theory delayed (p. 106); levels of the skill learning sequence (from pp. 111, 117, 126, 129, 136, 141); stepwise and bridging movement, Table 17 (pp. 230–231).; Hearing Harmony: four stages of readiness for chord changes (p. 305); harmonic patterns I V7 I, I IV I, I II V7 I, I II7 V7 I (p. 313); I V7 I, then I IV I, then I IV V7 I and I V7 IV I in three sung parts, then harmonic minor (pp. 318–319); easy and moderately difficult harmonic patterns, the supertonic delayed (p. 320).; Bass Lines by Ear: macrobeats in usual duple and triple meter (pp. 175–176); same is easier to hear than different (p. 219).

Mullen, Andy. The Literate Musician: How to Hear, Speak, Think, Read & Write the Language of Music. Revised 2nd ed., The Improving Musician, 2020. FPIFO, major and minor tonic and dominant (pp. 57, 59), copied into mullen-fpifo-major / -minor in apps/patterns/pattern-set.js; FPIFO in the Dorian, Mixolydian, Phrygian, Lydian, Aeolian and Locrian tonalities (pp. 22–27), mullen-fpifo-dorian … -locrian, with the keys moved so that C is the book’s resting tone; Major and Minor Subdominant FPIFO (p. 293), mullen-subdominant-major / -minor; the stepwise sets (pp. 71–72) are the site’s major-stepwise / minor-stepwise; rhythm patterns by lesson (duple and triple macrobeat and microbeat, pp. 37, 39–40; divisions, pp. 45, 47; elongation cells, pp. 48–49), copied into the mullen-rhythm-* sets of apps/rhythms/rhythm-pattern-object.js; translation lessons (Rhythm 8, 9.3, 10.3; Harmony 9); Hearing Harmony: Harmony lessons 2–5 (major and minor tonic and dominant, pp. 53–58), 7 (comparing major and minor, p. 62), the Harmonic Loops by tonality (pp. 20–27).
